cards.hint: act now or miss the chance
cards.meaning: There is an urgent need to act immediately because delay could mean missing an opportunity.
cards.nuance: It adds pressure and a sense of consequence, so it works well for deadlines or fast-moving situations. In casual conversation, it can sound dramatic if the situation is not truly urgent.

uses.sentence: We have no time to lose, so let’s identify the quickest way to get the product ready.
uses.tip: Follow it with a clear action so the urgency feels purposeful.

uses.sentence: Tickets are nearly gone, so we’ve got no time to lose if we want to go tonight.
uses.tip: It works naturally when the need to act is immediate and obvious.

uses.sentence: With the client arriving tomorrow, there is no time to lose on the remaining changes.
uses.tip: Use it in urgent internal updates, but provide the specific reason and next step.

origin.summary: The wording comes from the idea that wasting time also wastes a valuable chance to act. The phrase became established through its clear association with urgency.

timeline.text: The phrase developed from the literal idea that delay uses time that cannot be recovered.
Similar expressions about having no time to lose appeared in writing as urgency became a familiar way to describe immediate action.
It is common in work, news and everyday speech when someone wants to stress that action cannot wait.

cards.pitfall: Don’t use it when a task can wait; it can make a manageable deadline sound like a crisis.

cards.meaning: Used to emphasize that something someone has said is completely true.
cards.nuance: It sounds strong and relieved, often after admitting a surprising fact or confirming someone’s story. It is more conversational and emotional than simply saying “that’s true.”
cards.literal: Every word spoken is true, with no lie mixed in.

uses.sentence: The client approved the final budget without changing anything—there was no word of a lie.
uses.tip: Use it when you want to emphasize surprising good news.

uses.where: Listening to a friend · reacting to news
uses.sentence: She really did win the competition; there was no word of a lie.
uses.tip: It works best after an emphatic claim that might otherwise sound exaggerated.

uses.sentence: He really did complete the entire project on time—there was no word of a lie.
uses.tip: It suits personal messages better than formal reports or business emails.

origin.summary: Likely developed from older expressions such as “not a word of a lie” and “every word true,” which promise that a statement contains nothing false.

timeline.text: Related expressions used “every word true” and “not a word of a lie” to stress complete truthfulness.
The wording became established in conversation and popular writing.
It remains an emphatic, informal way to confirm that someone’s story is true.

similar: not a word of a lie
cards.pitfall: The phrase is very emphatic, so it can sound exaggerated or melodramatic in a serious situation.

cards.hint: not a different person, but one specific person
cards.meaning: Used to identify someone or something when the person or thing is unexpected or noteworthy.
cards.nuance: It adds emphasis and often a touch of surprise. It can sound admiring or dramatic, so use it selectively in formal writing.
cards.literal: Not a different person, but one specific person.

uses.sentence: The person who solved our production issue was none other than our new intern.
uses.tip: It works well when revealing an unexpected but relevant person.

uses.sentence: At the door was none other than my old neighbour, holding a bottle of wine.
uses.tip: Use it for a cheerful reveal when someone unexpected appears.

uses.sentence: The opening speaker was none other than the author whose book inspired the evening.
uses.tip: It adds a dramatic flourish, so keep the surrounding writing plain.

origin.summary: The phrase grew from the older construction “none other,” with the second “than” added to make comparison clearer. Its modern sense is well established, though the exact point when it became fixed is difficult to date.

timeline.text: “None” and “other” were combined to mean no person or thing besides the one named.
Forms of “none other than” appeared in English writing as a more explicit comparison.
The phrase is widely used to introduce an unexpected or noteworthy person or thing.

cards.pitfall: The phrase should identify a specific person or thing; using it with an abstract quality such as “none other than trouble” is usually comic or deliberately exaggerated.

cards.meaning: At a suitable or expected time, rather than earlier than necessary.
cards.nuance: This suggests that something is happening at the right moment, not that it is late. It often works as a reassuring response to someone who is worried about waiting.
cards.literal: The event has not happened earlier than the proper or expected time.

uses.sentence: Don’t worry about the delay; the announcement is not before time.
uses.tip: Use it to reassure someone that a planned change will happen when it is ready.

uses.where: Waiting for a friend · checking plans
uses.sentence: Relax, your friend is not before time; they’re probably stuck in traffic.
uses.tip: This is a gentle way to explain a delay without making it sound serious.

uses.sentence: The review is not before time, so we will send the final details once the checks are complete.
uses.tip: It can soften the message that someone will need to wait a little longer.

origin.summary: Likely developed from the literal idea that something should not happen before its proper time. The exact first recorded use is uncertain.

timeline.text: The phrase developed from “before time,” meaning ahead of the proper or expected time.
The expression became used in speech to describe things that were not premature.
It remains a natural, slightly formal way to comment on timing.

cards.pitfall: Use this only when the timing is appropriate; it does not mean that something is happening later than planned.

cards.meaning: Used to say that something will definitely not happen or must never be done.
cards.nuance: This is emphatic and slightly formal. It works best when you need to refuse something clearly or rule out an action completely.

uses.sentence: I won’t share the client’s data with anyone outside the team, not on any account.
uses.tip: Use it for a firm limit, especially when confidentiality matters.

uses.sentence: You are not borrowing my car tonight, not on any account.
uses.tip: It sounds stronger and more dramatic than simply saying “No.”

uses.where: Email to a supplier · rejecting an offer
uses.sentence: We cannot accept a delivery after Friday, not on any account.
uses.tip: Keep it in formal writing when an absolutely firm answer is needed.

origin.summary: Likely developed from older emphatic wording such as “on no account,” where “account” meant reason or consideration.

timeline.text: Older expressions used “account” in the sense of reason or grounds for an action.
Forms such as “on no account” became established ways of expressing an absolute refusal.
“Not on any account” remains a forceful, formal alternative to “never” or “under no circumstances.”

cards.pitfall: The phrase is very strong; it can sound dramatic in a minor situation, so use a gentler refusal when the point is not serious.

cards.meaning: Used to tell someone to wait and not act or assume something too quickly.
cards.nuance: Direct but playful, often used when correcting an assumption or interrupting a plan. It can sound dismissive if the reason for the pause is not explained.

uses.where: Team discussion · challenging a premature decision
uses.sentence: Not so fast—we should check the budget before promising a delivery date.
uses.tip: Follow it with a practical reason to soften the correction.

uses.where: Planning with friends · considering an expensive activity
uses.sentence: Not so fast; let’s ask how much the tickets cost before we book anything.
uses.tip: This light version works well when friends are moving too quickly.

uses.sentence: Not so fast—the deadline is still under review, so please don’t share the date yet.
uses.tip: Pair it with clear context so it does not feel abrupt in a formal message.

origin.summary: The wording has long been used as a brisk warning that someone is acting too quickly. Its familiar conversational form appears in English by the early 20th century.

timeline.text: The basic sense is a warning to stop or slow down.
“Not so fast” becomes established in English conversation as a brief response to premature action or confidence.
It remains a common way to pause someone, with a tone ranging from playful to firm.

cards.pitfall: It may sound like you are shutting down the discussion; briefly explain what needs checking first.

cards.term: not the brightest bulb in the chandelier
cards.meaning: Not very intelligent or quick to understand something.
cards.nuance: Humorous but potentially insulting, so it is best used among people who know each other well. It is usually about someone’s thinking rather than their general character.
cards.literal: A chandelier has several light bulbs, and this imagines that the speaker is not the brightest one.

uses.sentence: He may be not the brightest bulb in the chandelier, but he learns quickly once someone shows him the steps.
uses.highlight: not the brightest bulb in the chandelier
uses.tip: Use it gently with a colleague; it can sound insulting in a formal workplace.

uses.where: Teasing a friend over a puzzle
uses.sentence: I’m clearly not the brightest bulb in the chandelier because I’ve tried this puzzle three times.
uses.highlight: not the brightest bulb in the chandelier
uses.tip: A light self-deprecating joke can make the teasing feel friendly.

uses.sentence: I’m not the brightest bulb in the chandelier, so explain the trick again, please.
uses.highlight: not the brightest bulb in the chandelier
uses.tip: It works in an informal message but may be too mocking for professional correspondence.

origin.summary: The exact wording is not clearly recorded in standard etymologies. It likely developed as a more elaborate version of older light-bulb comparisons such as “the smartest bulb in the box.”

timeline.text: Light-bulb metaphors were used to describe intelligence, often comparing one person’s quick thinking with a duller one.
The “brightest bulb” comparison spread in informal English and was later extended with “in the chandelier.”
The full phrase remains a casual, mildly insulting idiom rather than standard business English.

similar: not the sharpest tool in the shed
not the smartest person in the room
a bit slow on the uptake
cards.pitfall: It can sound affectionate when you are teasing yourself or a close friend, but harsher when directed at a colleague or stranger.

cards.term: not the end of the world
cards.hint: a problem is serious, but manageable
cards.meaning: Used to reassure someone that a problem is serious but will not cause lasting harm.
cards.nuance: It can comfort people who are worried or apologetic, but it may sound dismissive if someone genuinely needs support.
cards.literal: The world continuing to exist after a frightening or difficult event.

uses.sentence: We missed the first deadline, but it’s not the end of the world—we can revise the plan today.
uses.highlight: not the end of the world
uses.tip: Acknowledge the problem before using this reassurance.

uses.sentence: Your flight got cancelled, but it’s not the end of the world; we can meet next weekend instead.
uses.highlight: not the end of the world
uses.tip: It works well when the inconvenience is minor and the mood is light.

uses.where: Email after a delay · managing expectations
uses.sentence: The delivery will arrive two days late, which is not the end of the world, and we’ll refund the shipping fee.
uses.highlight: not the end of the world
uses.tip: Pair it with a practical solution so it does not feel dismissive.

origin.summary: This phrase uses the idea of the world ending to describe a serious setback that is temporary rather than catastrophic.

timeline.text: People used dramatic expressions about the end of the world for extreme disaster or ruin.
The expression developed into a reassuring way to put a difficult situation into perspective.
It is common in everyday conversation to soften the impact of setbacks and mistakes.

cards.pitfall: Do not use it to dismiss someone’s genuine distress or a serious problem that still needs attention.

cards.term: not the sharpest crayon in the box
cards.meaning: Not very intelligent or quick to understand something.
cards.nuance: This is a playful but insulting way to describe someone as slow-witted. It can sound affectionate among close friends, but may be rude or unprofessional at work.
cards.literal: A crayon in a box that is blunt or worn, rather than sharpened to a fine point.

uses.where: Explaining a simple process · teasing a colleague
uses.sentence: You’re not the sharpest crayon in the box, but I’m happy to explain the steps again.
uses.highlight: not the sharpest crayon in the box
uses.tip: Keep this among colleagues who share an easygoing relationship; it can sound mocking in a formal workplace.

uses.where: Game night · joking about a wrong answer
uses.sentence: I guessed the first clue, so I’m clearly not the sharpest crayon in the box tonight.
uses.highlight: not the sharpest crayon in the box
uses.tip: Use it about yourself for self-deprecating humor rather than directly about someone else.

uses.where: Friendly message · teasing a close friend
uses.sentence: I’m not the sharpest crayon in the box, but I’m pretty sure that message was a joke.
uses.highlight: not the sharpest crayon in the box
uses.tip: It works best in informal writing with people who already know you well.

origin.summary: The wording is probably a playful American expansion of older expressions about being a dull pencil or not having a sharp mind. Its exact first use is difficult to pin down.

timeline.text: People used comparisons involving sharp pencils and dull minds to describe limited intelligence.
The phrase developed into a joking variation using “crayon in the box.”
It remains mainly informal and humorous, especially in American English.

similar: not the brightest bulb in the box
a bit slow on the uptake
cards.pitfall: This phrase directly labels someone as unintelligent, so avoid it in feedback, interviews, customer conversations or other sensitive situations.

cards.term: not the sharpest pencil in the box
cards.meaning: Not very intelligent, quick to understand, or able to make good decisions.
cards.nuance: This is a light, teasing way to describe someone who seems slow or has made a poor decision. It can sound insulting, so use it only with people you know well and when the mood is relaxed.
cards.literal: A dull pencil is less effective at writing than a sharp one, so the sharpest pencil in the box represents the cleverest person.

uses.where: Team discussion · explaining a simple process
uses.sentence: If the instructions are still unclear, maybe I should explain them again—I'm not the sharpest pencil in the box.
uses.highlight: not the sharpest pencil in the box
uses.tip: Use it about yourself to soften a misunderstanding, rather than aiming it at a colleague.

uses.where: Joking with friends · someone misses an obvious detail
uses.sentence: You locked your keys in the car? Well, you're not the sharpest pencil in the box today.
uses.highlight: not the sharpest pencil in the box
uses.tip: It works best as playful teasing among friends who can take a joke.

uses.sentence: I misunderstood the email, so I'm not the sharpest pencil in the box this morning.
uses.highlight: not the sharpest pencil in the box
uses.tip: Use it to admit a mistake without becoming overly formal or defensive.

origin.summary: The expression likely developed from the idea that a sharp pencil is more useful than a dull one. Its exact first use is not securely documented, but it became established as a teasing way to describe someone who is not quick-witted.

timeline.text: The literal image of the sharpest pencil in a box suggested the cleverest or most capable person.
The expression was used in informal speech to call someone slow-witted or not very bright.
It remains a casual, mildly insulting idiom, especially in speech and friendly teasing.

similar: a few bricks short of a full load
cards.opposite: one of the sharpest pencils in the box
cards.pitfall: It can sound genuinely rude, so avoid using it about a colleague, client, or anyone you do not know well.

cards.term: not the sharpest tool in the box
cards.meaning: Not very intelligent or quick to understand.
cards.nuance: It sounds teasing and informal, so use it with people you know well or when the criticism is clearly lighthearted.
cards.literal: A tool that is not especially sharp among the tools kept in a box.

uses.where: Team chat · untangling a confusing request
uses.sentence: Sorry, I’m not the sharpest tool in the box, but could you explain who owns this task?
uses.highlight: not the sharpest tool in the box
uses.tip: Use it about yourself to soften a request for clarification.

uses.where: Movie night · explaining a complex plot
uses.sentence: I’m not the sharpest tool in the box, so explain the time jump again.
uses.highlight: not the sharpest tool in the box
uses.tip: It works well as a playful admission that you’re confused.

uses.where: Informal message · asking for clearer instructions
uses.sentence: I’m not the sharpest tool in the box, so could you send the steps in a simpler order?
uses.highlight: not the sharpest tool in the box
uses.tip: Keep it in informal messages; it may sound insulting in formal correspondence.

origin.summary: Likely developed from older expressions comparing a dull tool with sharper ones in the same box. The familiar modern wording became established in British English during the 20th century.

timeline.text: The expression developed from comparisons between tools in a shared box.
The phrase became a familiar British way of describing someone who is not quick-witted.
It remains common in casual British and Australian speech, usually with playful or self-deprecating humour.

similar: not the sharpest knife in the drawer
a few bricks short of a full load
cards.pitfall: Even when meant lightly, this phrase can sound insulting, so avoid it when discussing someone’s intelligence directly.

cards.term: not the sharpest tool in the shed
cards.meaning: Not very intelligent or quick to understand something.
cards.nuance: This is a light, teasing way to describe someone’s lack of cleverness, often among friends or familiar colleagues. It can sound insulting in a serious or unfamiliar setting.
cards.literal: A shed contains tools, but not all of them are sharp or effective.

uses.where: Team discussion · explaining a simple process
uses.sentence: I repeated the instructions twice because he’s not the sharpest tool in the shed.
uses.highlight: not the sharpest tool in the shed
uses.tip: Keep this among colleagues you know well; it can sound mocking otherwise.

uses.sentence: Don’t take the wrong turn; you’re definitely not the sharpest tool in the shed.
uses.highlight: not the sharpest tool in the shed
uses.tip: It works best as affectionate teasing when there’s clear affection.

uses.where: Informal message to a friend · joking explanation
uses.sentence: I’m not the sharpest tool in the shed, but I think the meeting is tomorrow.
uses.highlight: not the sharpest tool in the shed
uses.tip: Use it in relaxed messages, not formal reports or feedback about a colleague.

origin.summary: This phrase comes from the idea that a shed contains useful tools, but some are blunt or worn out. The comparison for a clever person is well established, and the full expression is especially associated with Australian English.

timeline.text: People began comparing clever or capable people with sharp tools and ordinary people with blunt tools.
The wording developed in Australian English, where sheds and tool collections were familiar parts of everyday life.
The phrase is used in casual English to make a mild joke about someone’s intelligence.

similar: a bit slow on the uptake
cards.pitfall: This can sound affectionate between friends but rude when directed at a stranger, a client or someone you do not know well.

cards.hint: not allowing someone else to win
cards.meaning: Doing something equally impressive or more impressive in response to someone else’s achievement.
cards.nuance: It often expresses friendly rivalry or admiration, suggesting that one person or group tried to match or surpass another.
cards.literal: One competitor refusing to let another competitor do better.

uses.sentence: With rivals launching faster service, our product team was not to be outdone and began rebuilding the onboarding flow.
uses.tip: Use it when both sides achieved something impressive, not to dismiss the other team.

uses.where: Friendly competition at a bake sale
uses.sentence: When my friend organized a charity bake sale, I was not to be outdone and brought enough cookies for the whole office.
uses.tip: It adds playful rivalry to social stories involving sports, contests or personal achievements.

uses.sentence: Our volunteers were not to be outdone, so they arranged a second collection point for the busiest weekend.
uses.tip: It works well in light, energetic writing when describing matching or stronger efforts.

origin.summary: The phrase developed from “outdo,” an older word meaning to exceed or surpass someone. Its exact first appearance is difficult to pin down, but it became established as a way of describing competitive effort during the 19th century.

timeline.text: The word “outdo” emerges in English with the sense of surpassing or doing better than someone else.
The wording “not to be outdone” becomes established for refusing to remain behind a competitor.
It is used in friendly and professional contexts to describe matching or exceeding another effort.

cards.pitfall: The phrase usually implies friendly rivalry; using it about a serious conflict can make the tone sound too playful.

cards.hint: a playful way to introduce good news
cards.meaning: Used before sharing a success or piece of good news to sound modest and playful.
cards.nuance: It often makes the person sound pleased rather than seriously self-effacing. It works best with friends or people you know, but can feel insincere in a formal setting.
cards.literal: The words suggest that claiming to brag would be unfair because what comes next is so impressive.

uses.sentence: Not to brag, but our team handled the busiest sales day without any delays.
uses.tip: Keep it light with colleagues; it can undermine a serious update.

uses.sentence: Not to brag, but I finally finished that novel everyone said would take me forever.
uses.tip: Use it when the good news is genuinely worth celebrating.

uses.sentence: Not to brag, but my presentation went so smoothly that nobody asked me a single question.
uses.tip: It suits personal messages better than formal work emails.

origin.summary: This is a modern playful disclaimer attached to the older English word “brag.” Its exact first use is not clearly documented, but it developed as a way to share good news while appearing modest.

timeline.text: The word “brag” was already used for boasting or speaking proudly about an achievement.
“Not to brag” emerged in informal speech as a humorous prelude to a boast.
It remains common in casual conversation, online posts and personal messages.

similar: if I do say so myself
cards.pitfall: It can sound fake if you use it before genuinely modest news or say it whenever you want attention.

cards.meaning: Used to emphasize that something is completely, entirely, or surprisingly impressive enough to be called something stronger.
cards.nuance: It adds emphasis and can sound admiring, surprised, or occasionally critical. It works naturally before a noun, such as “a success,” but avoid using it too often because it can make your praise sound dramatic.

uses.sentence: The team’s response to the deadline was nothing short of impressive.
uses.tip: Use it to emphasize genuinely exceptional effort or performance.

uses.sentence: Your cooking was nothing short of delicious; everyone asked for the recipe.
uses.tip: This sounds enthusiastic and natural when you want to make a warm compliment.

uses.sentence: Her contribution was nothing short of a turning point for the project.
uses.tip: It is formal enough for a review, but follow it with a specific example.

origin.summary: The phrase comes from an older expression meaning “no less than,” used for something that is equal to or more than expected.

timeline.text: The expression “nothing short of” appears in English with the meaning “no less than.”
It develops into a way of emphasizing admiration, surprise, or strong approval.
It remains common in spoken and formal English for emphatic praise or description.

cards.pitfall: “Nothing short of” is stronger than a simple compliment, so reserve it for results or qualities that truly deserve emphasis.

cards.meaning: Used to get someone’s full attention before giving an important message or instruction.
cards.nuance: Direct and emphatic, so it can feel playful among friends but bossy or impatient at work. Use it when you want the other person to stop talking and listen.
cards.literal: Listen to what is being said right now.

uses.sentence: Now hear this, the report is moving to Friday, so everyone needs to update their figures today.
uses.tip: It works best when followed by a clear, specific instruction.

uses.where: Conversation with a friend · sharing news
uses.sentence: Now hear this, we’re finally going to that new restaurant on Saturday.
uses.tip: This adds friendly excitement when you already have the listener’s attention.

uses.sentence: Now hear this: the invoice goes to Accounts, not Finance, until our system changes.
uses.tip: In writing, it may sound dramatic, so keep the message brief and professional.

origin.summary: The exact phrase is hard to trace, but it combines older wording such as “hear this” with the common attention-getter “now.” Its present-day force comes from sounding like a firm announcement.

timeline.text: The expression “hear this” was used to direct attention to an important point.
Forms such as “now hear this” became associated with emphatic public announcements and personal reminders.
It remains informal and is mainly used to add emphasis or drama.

cards.pitfall: It can sound bossy, sarcastic or melodramatic, especially with colleagues you do not know well.

cards.meaning: An enthusiastic way to say that something is exactly the right kind of thing.
cards.nuance: It sounds approving and often a little surprised or excited. It works best with friends or colleagues you know well, and can feel exaggerated or judgmental in formal settings.

uses.where: Team celebration · a colleague solves a problem
uses.sentence: Now that's what I call a smart solution—it saved us hours.
uses.tip: Reserve it for genuine praise; it can sound too familiar with senior colleagues.

uses.where: Friend's dinner party · tasting the food
uses.sentence: Now that's what I call dessert; I could eat a second bowl.
uses.tip: Use it to show playful enthusiasm in a relaxed conversation.

uses.where: Team chat · praising a finished presentation
uses.sentence: Now that's what I call a clear summary—easy to read and right on point.
uses.tip: It adds energy to informal messages but may not suit a formal report.

origin.summary: The exact origin is uncertain. It likely grew from ordinary English emphasis: “now” adds surprise, while “that's what I call” introduces a strong personal judgment.

timeline.text: People used “that's what I call” to identify or characterize something.
Adding “now” became a way to combine that statement with immediate enthusiasm.
The phrase remains common in casual speech as an emphatic expression of approval.

similar: just the way I like it
cards.pitfall: It can sound sarcastic if your approval is not obvious, so make your positive tone clear.

cards.meaning: An informal way of saying that someone is doing something well and has found the right approach.
cards.nuance: It sounds enthusiastic and encouraging, often with a playful sense of approval. It suits social conversation and relaxed workplace banter better than formal writing.
cards.literal: You are now preparing the food successfully, so the meal will be good.

uses.sentence: Now you're cooking—those three changes should solve the reporting problem.
uses.tip: Use it with colleagues you know well; it can sound too familiar in formal settings.

uses.sentence: Now you're cooking! That final ingredient makes the whole meal taste fantastic.
uses.tip: It works well as a cheerful reaction when someone improves a recipe.

uses.sentence: Now you're cooking—the revised opening is clear, direct, and actually engaging.
uses.tip: Keep it in a friendly message or chat, not in formal business correspondence.

origin.summary: Probably grew from the literal idea of cooking a successful meal and spread as casual praise for doing something well. Its precise starting point is unclear.

timeline.text: The literal expression connected successful cooking with a good result.
The figurative meaning developed: someone is performing a task successfully.
It remains a familiar, playful phrase of approval in American English and informal online speech.

similar: that's the way to do it
cards.opposite: now you're in over your head
cards.pitfall: The usual wording is “Now you're cooking,” without “now” before “you're”; avoid saying “Now you are cooking” if you mean the phrase.

cards.meaning: Used when someone says something you strongly agree with or proposes something sensible.
cards.nuance: It sounds enthusiastic and approving, but is usually more casual than professional. In a serious discussion, state your agreement more clearly instead.
cards.literal: The other person is finally speaking in a way that makes sense or appeals to you.

uses.where: Team discussion · choosing a practical solution
uses.sentence: We should focus on the two biggest problems first. Now you're talking.
uses.tip: Use it for clear approval, not for a suggestion that still needs discussion.

uses.where: Planning with friends · suggesting an easy option
uses.sentence: Let's order one pizza and share it. Now you're talking.
uses.tip: It works well with friends when you want to show enthusiastic agreement.

uses.sentence: A ten-minute walk before dinner? Now you're talking.
uses.tip: Keep it in relaxed messages; it may sound too playful for formal writing.

origin.summary: The exact origin is unclear, but the phrase probably developed from the idea that someone is finally saying what the listener wants to hear.

timeline.text: Its wording reflects a direct response to what another person has just said.
The approving conversational meaning becomes established in English.
It remains a common informal expression of enthusiastic agreement.

cards.pitfall: It can sound dismissive if used when someone is only partly understood, so make sure you genuinely approve before saying it.

cards.register: Common at work and in everyday speech
cards.meaning: Extremely high, large, or beyond normal limits.
cards.nuance: It emphasizes how unusual or extreme something is, often a number, price, demand, or change. It is usually informal and can sound more vivid than simply saying “enormous” or “unprecedented.”
cards.literal: Past the highest or normal markings on a measuring scale.

uses.sentence: The number of customer requests is off the scale, so we need more support this week.
uses.tip: Use it for figures or conditions that are clearly far beyond what is normal.

uses.sentence: That concert ticket price is off the scale—would you actually pay that much?
uses.tip: It works well in casual conversation when a price or cost seems extreme.

uses.sentence: Website traffic is off the scale following the product launch.
uses.tip: In a report, pair it with the exact figure so the claim is clear.

origin.summary: Probably developed from the idea of a measuring instrument showing a value beyond its normal range. The figurative use became established in the 20th century.

timeline.text: Literal sense: beyond the markings or limits of a measuring scale.
Figurative use spreads for numbers and conditions far beyond ordinary limits.
A common informal way to describe extreme size, cost, demand, or change.

cards.pitfall: “Off the scale” can sound vague, so include the actual number or situation when precision matters.

cards.hint: very close to a serious danger
cards.meaning: In a situation so dangerous or severe that death seems extremely close.
cards.nuance: This sounds urgent and serious, often suggesting that something bad is about to happen or has almost already happened. It is stronger and more dramatic than saying someone is simply in danger.
cards.literal: Standing directly outside the doorway of a person who has died.

uses.where: Operations meeting · reporting a critical failure
uses.sentence: If we lose the backup system tonight, the company will be on death's doorstep.
uses.tip: Use it for an extreme emergency, not an ordinary workplace problem.

uses.where: Conversation about a serious health scare
uses.sentence: After the crash, he was on death's doorstep before the paramedics arrived.
uses.tip: It adds drama, so consider whether the situation is truly that severe.

uses.where: News report · describing a dramatic turnaround
uses.sentence: With two minutes left, the team was on death's doorstep before scoring the winning goal.
uses.tip: It works in headlines and vivid reporting, but may sound overdramatic elsewhere.

origin.summary: Likely developed from older expressions such as “at death's door,” using “doorstep” to emphasize how close death is.

timeline.text: Related expressions referred to being close to death, including “at death's door.”
The wording “on death's doorstep” appears in dramatic accounts of peril and near-fatal events.
It remains a vivid, dramatic idiom for an extremely dangerous or critical situation.

cards.pitfall: This phrase is more dramatic than “in danger”; using it for a minor risk may sound exaggerated.

cards.register: Common at work and in everyday life
cards.meaning: Very close to reaching a particular state or taking a particular action.
cards.nuance: It creates tension and suggests that something important is about to happen. It is usually followed by “of” and a gerund, such as “on the verge of quitting.”

uses.sentence: We’re on the verge of missing the launch deadline unless we reduce the scope.
uses.tip: Use “of” before the action: “on the verge of missing.”

uses.sentence: I was on the verge of ordering dessert when you suggested we walk instead.
uses.tip: This gives a natural sense of a moment that nearly arrived.

uses.sentence: The team is on the verge of completing the final review, pending one approval.
uses.tip: Pair it with a specific remaining step so the status is clear.

origin.summary: The phrase comes from the literal edge of a place or surface and gradually came to mean being close to a new state or action.

timeline.text: “Verge” referred to an edge, boundary or the act of approaching something.
The expression began appearing in contexts meaning at or close to an edge.
“On the verge of” is widely used to describe being close to an important or dramatic change.

cards.pitfall: “On the verge” normally needs “of” and an action in the -ing form; avoid “on the verge to” unless you are directly naming something.

cards.term: on your mark, get set, go
cards.meaning: A command used to tell everyone to get ready and start.
cards.nuance: It adds energy and a sense of anticipation, often to a race, game or group activity. It can also be used playfully when beginning a task.
cards.literal: Stand on your starting mark, prepare yourself, and begin.

uses.where: Team sprint · starting a timed task
uses.sentence: On your mark, get set, go—we’ve got ten minutes to finish the first draft.
uses.highlight: On your mark, get set, go
uses.tip: Use it to add urgency, but make sure everyone knows the task.

uses.where: Family game night · starting a race
uses.sentence: On your mark, get set, go—the first person across the line gets dessert.
uses.highlight: On your mark, get set, go
uses.tip: It works well as a playful countdown before a competitive activity.

uses.sentence: On your mark, get set, go—the doors open at eight, and the opening performance starts right away.
uses.highlight: On your mark, get set, go
uses.tip: Keep it informal; it suits invitations and announcements rather than serious notices.

origin.summary: The phrase grew from separate commands used in races and shooting games. “On your mark” told competitors to stand at a mark, while “get set” called for readiness before the starting signal.

timeline.text: “On your mark” meant moving to a fixed starting position before a race or shooting competition.
The commands began combining into a familiar three-part starting signal.
The phrase is used for races, games, challenges and playful calls to begin.

cards.pitfall: For the full phrase, use “On your mark” as the opening part; “Mark your place, get set, go” changes the meaning.

cards.term: once a thief, always a thief
cards.hint: a person keeps their old ways
cards.meaning: Someone who has behaved dishonestly before may be expected to do so again.
cards.nuance: This expresses a belief that people do not change their basic habits or character. It can sound judgmental, so use it only when discussing a specific pattern of behaviour.
cards.literal: A person who has stolen once will be treated as a thief forever.

uses.sentence: He changed the invoice twice, so I’m wary: once a thief, always a thief.
uses.highlight: once a thief, always a thief
uses.tip: Use it to justify caution, but base it on clear evidence.

uses.sentence: He borrowed my bike and never returned it; once a thief, always a thief.
uses.highlight: once a thief, always a thief
uses.tip: It can sound harsh when aimed at someone you know personally.

uses.sentence: The company hid the safety defects for years—once a thief, always a thief.
uses.highlight: once a thief, always a thief
uses.tip: Keep the claim tied to repeated, documented conduct.

origin.summary: This is an old proverb-style warning that dishonest or criminal behaviour tends to continue. Its exact first use is uncertain, but the saying was already established in English by the 17th century.

timeline.text: The proverb developed from the broader idea that people remain known by their past conduct.
The wording was recorded in collections of English proverbs.
It remains a common warning about repeated dishonesty, though often in casual or rhetorical contexts.

similar: a leopard can't change its spots
you can't teach an old dog new tricks
cards.pitfall: The saying treats a past mistake as proof of permanent character, so it can prejudge someone; consider the actual evidence instead.

cards.register: Common at work and in everyday conversation
cards.meaning: One person in a group whose behavior harms the whole group or spoils an otherwise good situation.
cards.nuance: It often criticizes one disruptive individual, but it can sound harsh or unfair because it focuses on a person rather than the underlying problem.
cards.literal: A single rotten apple can make other apples nearby rot.

uses.sentence: We’ve had a productive quarter, but one bad apple has made the whole team dread our meetings.
uses.tip: Use it for serious, persistent disruption, not a minor disagreement.

uses.sentence: We were having a lovely time until one bad apple started making comments about everyone else.
uses.tip: It adds a blunt, slightly humorous edge to a complaint.

uses.sentence: I don’t want to label anyone, but one bad apple can quickly undermine trust across the entire group.
uses.tip: Pair it with specific, fair examples so it does not seem like a personal attack.

origin.summary: This phrase probably grew from the older proverb that one rotten apple spoils the whole basket. Its connection to apples is old, but the exact source of the modern wording is uncertain.

timeline.text: A traditional warning appeared in various forms: one spoiled apple can affect the fruit stored beside it.
Short versions comparing the idea to a bad apple or a rotten apple became common in English.
“One bad apple” labels a disruptive person whose conduct affects the wider group.

cards.pitfall: The expression can sound insulting and may oversimplify a wider problem; describe the behavior rather than labeling the person.
